title: The ladder of humility (ch. 7)
hook: twelve steps, rising by going down

segments.voice: Yesterday, restraint of speech: even good words, held back sometimes, for silence's sake. Your line was fewer words.

A ladder is about the simplest machine there is. Put your foot on the bottom rung, push, and you're higher. Up is up. Nobody has ever climbed a ladder by stepping down it. Chapter seven of Saint Benedict's Rule is built around a ladder, but this one works backward. On Benedict's ladder, the people who try to climb end up lower, and the ones who step down find themselves rising.
screen: `UP IS UP.` → `A LADDER THAT WORKS BACKWARD.` → `STEP DOWN TO RISE.`

segments.voice: Benedict opens the chapter with Jesus's words in Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "every one that exalteth himself, shall be humbled; and he that humbleth himself, shall be exalted." Then he reaches back to Genesis, to Jacob asleep on a stone, dreaming of a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down. Benedict reads the dream his own way. Going down is what happens when we lift ourselves up; going up is what happens when we bend low. The ladder is our life. Its two side rails are body and soul, and between them God has set the rungs. Benedict counts twelve. The first is to keep the fear of God before your eyes and never forget it. You've met others this week: obedience is one rung, and holding back from too much talk is another. Some rungs are gentle: patience when things are hard, being content with the plain and ordinary. Some are hard for a modern ear, like counting yourself lower than others, and readers today take those steps in different ways. The last rung is humility that shows in the body itself, in how a person walks and stands. And the surprise at the top: once all these steps are climbed, Benedict says, the monk arrives at the love of God that casts out fear, quoting the first letter of John: "perfect charity casteth out fear." The ladder starts with fear and ends with love. Humility, for Benedict, isn't thinking badly of yourself. It's getting out of your own way, until what's left is love, done easily, out of habit and delight.
screen: `WHO EXALTS HIMSELF SHALL BE HUMBLED.` · `JACOB'S LADDER, READ BACKWARD.` · `TWELVE RUNGS, FROM FEAR OF GOD UP.` · `AT THE TOP, LOVE THAT CASTS OUT FEAR.` · then, large: `PERFECT CHARITY CASTETH OUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: Look at the day ahead for one small seat you could take that's a step down: letting someone go first, passing the credit to the person who helped, the worse parking spot, the smaller slice. Picture doing it quietly, without anyone noticing you chose it, and if something in you resists, let it, and breathe out. If you pray, offer that small step down to God.
Humility. For Benedict, a ladder you rise on by stepping down, with twelve rungs and love at the top. Today's word.
Your line: down is up. On Benedict's ladder, the top rung is love, not fear. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns hear chapter seven read in community, and some Catholics outside monasteries use its twelve steps as an examination of conscience.
